course_description:
Peacebuilding is an extraordinarily complex cross-cultural international venture. Moreover, it has emerged only recently as a recognised domain of policy and risen rapidly into prominence. Drawing on scholarly writing, case studies and role plays, this course examines some of the elements that make up peacebuilding and explores some of the political, ethical and practical dilemmas that characterise efforts to rebuild the society and political community of others.

In the decades following the Cold War’s end, peacebuilding acquired increasing prominence as an international means for responding to violent conflict and an instrument for preventing its recurrence. Peacebuilding is a valuable, complex and unavoidably political endeavour, subject to often conflicting policy frameworks, moral imperatives, end-goals, and practical methods.

This course delves deeply into the aims, dilemmas, paradoxes, weaknesses, and opportunities of contemporary peacebuilding. A problem-led syllabus prompts students to develop their own critical understanding of peacebuilding practices, as well as the most promising avenues for building peace. Putting a central political dilemma of peacebuilding at the heart of our enquiry—the tension between the undeniably international drivers of peacebuilding policy and the fundamentally local drivers of peace itself—students will be encouraged to apply a set of analytical tools and insights to their own areas of peacebuilding interest.

By charting the historical development of peacebuilding policy and the evolution of ideas about its practice, students will develop an empirical understanding of past attempts to build peace, critically analyse international policymaking processes, and explain change and continuity in peacebuilding policy. The course will also foster nuanced understanding of the theories of change underpinning different peacebuilding modalities as well as of the contradictions that often characterise contemporary peacebuilding efforts. Students will analyse the distinctive agendas, methods and contributions of the diverse range of peacebuilders, including the United Nations, international agencies, civil society, national actors, and women and young people.

Throughout the course, students are encouraged to bring a practical, real-world lens to bear on the study of peacebuilding’s many problems. How can peacebuilding work better? How should we evaluate efforts to build peace in some of the most difficult operating environments? What theories of success and failure can illuminate promising options for peacebuilding reform? What will it take to generate game-changing innovation to improve the impact of peacebuilding efforts?

course_aims: This course aims to introduce students to key elements of peacebuilding, to encourage a reflective, critical and practical appreciation of some of the ethical and political dilemmas that characterise it, and to explore ways of working with those dilemmas.

learning_outcomes.description: Identify and understand different dimensions of and approaches to peacebuilding.
Understand and explain some of the key ideas and assumptions associated with different approaches to peacebuilding.
Have some practical and theoretical appreciation of ethical and political dilemmas involved in peacebuilding.
Be aware of and able to articulate the challenges of working across cultures - conceptually and in concrete terms.
Synthesise, analyse and critically assess key concepts and arguments presented in the relevant literature.
Demonstrate, through research and communication, your understanding of the field.

assessment_details.title: In-Class Quiz
assessment_details.task_description: Reading the required texts in the course's reading list is essential for coming prepared to class and for success in POLS7505. In each seminar in Weeks 2-7, you will be given 10 minutes to complete a short, handwritten, closed book quiz. The precise timing of the quiz during the seminar's 4-hour window may vary week-by-week. Each quiz is worth 5 marks, divided in two parts. The first part will ask you to define a key concept of one of the readings (worth a maximum 2 pts). The second part will ask you to explain how this concept helps to understand or critically assess peacebuilding practice, based on the key points the author(s) made in the reading (worth a maximum 3 pts). While there are 6 opportunities to take the quiz, only 4 will count towards your final mark, up to a maximum of 20%. Your top 4 results will comprise your mark if you take more than 4 quizzes. Since this allows you to miss up to two of the six quizzes, you will not be able to re-sit individual quizzes and no alternative assessment will be available. If you have a disability plan that prevents you from taking hand-written quizzes, please get in touch with the course's staff as soon as possible to find suitable arrangements. Special consideration for alternative assessment will only be given under highly unusual and well-documented circumstances, to students who are unable to attend more than one seminar during which quizzes are taking place. As there'll be only one opportunity to take an alternative quiz, please let the course coordinator know no later than 4 September and provide all the necessary documentation. Please note: This assessment task is to be completed in person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempt to use AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Peace Process Evaluation-Group Report
assessment_details.task_description: Peace processes are inherently complex and politically fraught, and even successful negotiations rarely translate into sustained and uncontested peace. The relative effectiveness of a peace proccess is shaped by how it was designed and implemented, who participated, and whether it was able to address the underlying drivers as well as legacies of armed conflict and mass violence. Working in groups, students will produce a 4000 word evaluation report of a historical or contemporary peace process (e.g., Bougainville, Aceh, Myanmar, Mindanao, South Sudan, Colombia, Nepal, etc.) that assesses the conflict context, peace process, and peace agreement (where applicable), and critically evaluates peace implementation with respect to sustainable peacebuilding outcomes. Your report should draw on relevant evidence and literature to explain and critically evaluate: the drivers and dynamics of the conflict; the objectives and design of the peace process; the roles of relevant national, local, regional, and international actors; how key issues such as security, governance, justice, reconciliation, power-sharing, and development were addressed; challenges to implementation; the extent to which the peace process has contributed to sustainable peace; and the key lessons the case offers for future peacebuilding efforts in that or other contexts. Please consult the marking criteria sheet in Blackboard for more information on expectations. Citation practice should conform to the standards set out in the School of Political Science and International Studies Essay Guide . Please note: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use Al and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative Al or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of Al and MT tools. assessment_details.title: Peace Process Evaluation-Group Presentation
assessment_details.task_description: You will present the findings of your peace process evaluation to the class in a 15-minute group powerpoint presentation during our final seminar in Week 7. Your presentation will be followed by a Q&A, in which each group member will be asked to respond to a question by the course coordinator. Presentations will be recorded. You should supplement your presentation with a 1-2 page 'explainer' handout for the class. The handout should succinctly communicate your group's key findings and analysis using a clear, accessible, and visually engaging format. The aim is to highlight the most important insights from your presentation rather than reproduce it in full. This assignment is worth 20 marks: 10 are based on the quality of the group presentation; 10 are based the quality of your individual response to questions. The questions will be intended to assess your knowledge of the peace process, the key debates that informed your analysis, and the sources and academic literature you used. Your group may also be asked to respond to questions from the instructor and classmates about your use of AI. You should upload your powerpoint presentation to TurnitIn by 5pm on the day of your presentation. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Peacebuilding Philosophy Statement
assessment_details.task_description: This assignment invites you to develop a 2500 word Peacebuilding Philosophy Statement that articulates and defends your own approach to peacebuilding by synthesising relevant theories, concepts, debates, and lessons we've examined throughout the course. Task Description: Your task is to develop a clear, critical, and evidence-informed statement of your peacebuiding philosophy and explain how it would inform your approach to professional practice. Your statement should address the following: Analyse the contemporary peacebuilding landscape by identifying the key drivers of violent conflict and the principal challenges to building and sustaining peace. You may focus your analysis on a specific conflict context or examine broader cross-cutting challenges affecting peacebuilding globally. Critically assess the role of peacebuilding practitioners in this context by evaluating the knowledge, skills, attributes and approaches required to respond effectively to these challenges. Evaluate what constitutes good peacebuilding practice: critically assess the principles, practices, and approaches most appropriate to contemporary peacebuilding contexts; Identify gaps, blind spots, or emerging challenges that may be limiting peacebuilding effectiveness (e.g. what should this course, the UQ PACS program, or the wider peacebuilding field be addressing that it currently isn't?); Reflect on the constraints and ethical, political, and practical dilemmas that peacebuilding practitioners must navigate, including the tensions and trade-offs between competing objectives or priorities in complex conflict settings; Based on this analysis, Articulate and defend your own philosophy of peacebuilding , explaining (1) how it has been informed by this course, relevant scholarship, your lived experience, or other formative influences, and (2) how it would guide your approach to peacebuilding practice or other professional contexts. The aim of this assessment is to produce a critical and scholarly statement that demonstrates your ability to synthesise the course material and relevant literature into a coherent, theoretically grounded, and evidence-informed philosophy of peacebuilding. While you may choose to reflect on how your own identity, personal background, or positionality has shaped your perspective, this is not simply an autobiographical or personal reflection. Your arguments should be supported by relevant academic literature and demonstrate critical engagement with contemporary peacebuilding debates. The citation practice in the Statement should conform to the standards set out in the School of Political Science and International Studies Essay Guide . Please consult the criteria sheet in Blackboard for more information on expectations. Please note: This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex.
